summary: This informational document lists requirements for a service that lets applications subscribe to updates of a YANG datastore. Once a subscription is negotiated, changes are pushed to the chosen recipients instead of the application polling over and over. It points out that existing YANG transports such as NETCONF and RESTCONF lack this publish and subscribe capability.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7923 describes what a service for subscribing to YANG datastore updates should support. The goal is to push changes to interested applications instead of having them poll repeatedly.

subtitle: Requirements for pushing updates from YANG datastores to subscribers

tldr.problem: Applications that need current YANG datastore information often poll devices. Polling adds load and can miss or delay changes.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets requirements for subscriptions that negotiate the data, update policy, filters, transport, and quality of service, then push updates to a receiver.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7923 describes requirements and terminology for a subscription service. It does not specify a protocol.

today: RFC 7923 is an Informational requirements document and the batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It sets requirements for a YANG datastore subscription service, not a protocol.

sections.title: Why Push Updates
sections.content:
Service-assurance applications need a continuing view of operational data. Security applications may need to track configuration changes to check whether devices follow policy. Periodically fetching data can load networks, devices, and applications, and missed polling cycles can make the result unreliable.

The RFC proposes a generic subscription capability for YANG datastore data. A publisher sends updates to recipients according to criteria negotiated when a subscription is created. Push distribution supplements existing management protocols rather than replacing them.
sections.plainLanguage: Repeated polling uses network and device resources and may miss changes between checks. A subscription lets a device send updates when requested conditions are met.

sections.title: Subscriber, Publisher, and Receiver
sections.content:
A Subscriber requests YANG object data. A Publisher, generally the datastore owner, distributes the data under the subscription terms. A Receiver gets the pushed updates and is usually the same entity as the Subscriber. The Subscription Service provides subscriptions and works with the Publisher.

A subscription specifies the data to send and its terms. An Update carries changes within subscribed data. A Filter selects data by subtree or by properties of objects and their attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: The subscriber requests data, the publisher provides it, and the receiver gets the updates. Often the subscriber and receiver are the same application.

sections.title: Subscription and Update Requirements
sections.content:
A Subscription Service MUST create, renew, time out, and terminate subscriptions, and independently track multiple requests from one Subscriber. It MUST support configuration and operational datastores, periodic updates, configurable periods, and filters. It SHOULD support on-change updates; for those, it MUST support a dampening period and send only changed data, marked as added, changed, or removed.

The service negotiates the update policy, interval, dampening period, and filters. If it cannot meet a request, it SHOULD suggest acceptable criteria. It MAY suspend or revoke a subscription, but it MUST notify the Subscriber and update the subscription status. Updates must not be sent before dampening expires or later than the applicable push-latency or dampening limit.
sections.plainLanguage: A subscription can request timed updates or updates after changes, with filters and timing limits. If the service suspends or revokes it, the subscriber must be notified.

sections.title: Transport, Quality, and Filtering
sections.content:
The service SHOULD support different transports and payload encodings. A receiver MUST be able to associate each update with its subscription. Updates for an object MUST arrive in sequence. The RFC also describes negotiated reliability, deadlines, bundling, dampening, push latency, and relative priority.

Filters MUST support subtree and object properties. For character data, required comparisons include equal, not equal, and contains; numeric filters MUST support =, !=, <, <=, >, and >=. The service MUST expose the state of one subscription, all subscriptions for a subscriber, and subscription request history with failure reasons.
sections.plainLanguage: Subscribers can choose which data to receive and how updates should be delivered. The service must support filters, ordered updates, and ways to inspect subscription status.

sections.title: Authentication and Authorization
sections.content:
For privacy-sensitive deployments, subscription data MUST use secure, encrypted transport. Mutual authentication MUST be used between the Subscriber and Subscription Service, and Subscribers MUST NOT be able to pose as the service.

Pushed data MUST be authorized as for ordinary data retrieval and filtered to exclude data the Receiver cannot read. Requests to create, terminate, suspend, or resume subscriptions must be authorized. The service SHOULD decline requests likely to exhaust its resources.
sections.plainLanguage: The service must authenticate both sides and send only data the receiver is allowed to read. It should reject subscriptions likely to exhaust its resources.
